problem: Existing zero-shot ObjectNav methods rely on a single robot's egocentric view, which has limited coverage and makes exploration inefficient in large multi-floor environments. There was no dataset or framework for robots collaborating with indoor surveillance cameras.
motivation: Surveillance systems are widely deployed in factories, offices and homes. Collaborative perception has already helped autonomous driving, so it should also help indoor navigation. Fixed cameras give a static global view but have blind spots, while a robot gives dynamic local sensing.
key_idea: Fuse a robot's egocentric RGB-D with multi-view surveillance cameras into joint 3D/2D maps, CLIP value maps and a joint 3D object map, so the agent can head directly to targets seen by cameras and verify them across sources.
insight: Adding surveillance input gives the largest gain: FMM goes from 26.1/62.7 to 34.5/67.4 (SPL/SR), and the SP planner from 28.0/68.7 to 36.4/71.1. Panoramic coverage and denser cameras help modestly (SPL 32.1 to 34.5, and 33.0 to 34.5). Region-centric CLIP value maps beat greedy and object-centric ones, and the GroundingDINO detector beats YOLO-World (SR 67.4 vs 59.0). Remaining bottlenecks are occlusion, camera placement and false detections.
method: Active Camera Invocation: activates only surveillance cameras whose estimated floor height is within a threshold (0.4 m) of the agent's floor, which filters cross-floor cameras and cuts computation.

Joint 3D Point Cloud Map: back-projects robot RGB-D and fixed-camera RGB-D (GT depth, known poses) into a global frame and merges them. It is projected to an obstacle map and an exploration map, with frontiers obtained by dilation and subtraction.

Joint Value Map: computes CLIP cosine similarity between each image and the prompt 'seems like there is a [object]', projects it to the top-down map using depth and pose, and averages the surveillance and robot values per cell.

Joint 3D Object Map: uses Grounding DINO with MobileSAM masks and CLIP crop features to make semantic point clouds. New detections are associated by a weighted sum of feature similarity and point-cloud IoU (threshold 1.35), and matched objects are fused.

Joint Object Confirmation: takes the object confidence as the max over robot and camera observations. It confirms a target above a threshold, and treats a category change over time as a false positive.

Waypoint Selection and Navigation: goes to the confirmed target, or else to a low-confidence candidate object or the highest-value frontier. FMM or a shortest-path (SP) planner handles local navigation.

Dataset: builds a Habitat HM3Dv2 dataset with floor identification by DBSCAN, one camera per 100 m² at 1.8 m height chosen by farthest point sampling, and 13 views per camera at 1280x1280 RGB-D. It has 1,000 episodes over 36 scenes, 74 floors and 206 cameras, with the 6 standard ObjectNav categories.

setting.backbone: CLIP (frozen) for value maps, Grounding DINO + MobileSAM (frozen) for detection and segmentation, FMM/SP planner
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (640x480, 79° FOV) with pose, plus RGB-D and poses from surveillance cameras (1280x1280, 100° FOV)
setting.action_space: low-level: move forward 0.25 m, turn left/right 30°, look up/down 30°, stop (max 500 steps)
setting.privileged: GT depth for surveillance cameras, known camera poses and agent pose, and the surveillance cameras' observations from all cameras

numbers_note: The split is not stated in the paper; 'val' is assumed, and the results are on the authors' own 1,000-episode surveillance dataset built from HM3Dv2. The baseline numbers are taken from MCoCoNav, so the comparison is only approximate.
results: With surveillance, the SP variant reaches 36.4 SPL / 71.1 SR and the FMM variant 34.5 / 67.4. The strongest reported baseline is MCoCoNav (29.7 / 63.4), and VLN-Game reaches 26.9 / 66.7. Removing surveillance drops performance clearly, especially SPL (by about 8 points).
limitations: Relies on precise camera poses and GT depth for the surveillance cameras, and was evaluated only in simulation with static environments.
Occlusions, sub-optimal camera placement and detector false positives cap the gains, even with dense cameras.
Communication bandwidth and latency in real deployments are not addressed.
